This contemporary play is about highschoolers reading Arthur Miller’s The Crucible, which tells of the most famous witchhunts of all time. This is a fun choice, and it’s refreshing to have a non-horror adjacent play during the month of Halloween.
John Proctor is the Villain was written in 2022 and made it to Broadway in 2025 starring Sadie Sink. After receiving seven Tony nominations, it is now, with producers including Sadie Sink and Tina Fey, in development to become a film under the Broadway show’s original director, Danya Taymor.  The Nashville Repertory Theatre is performing this play in Johnson Theater, the black-box theater downstairs at TPAC, and the crowd was full when I attended
Lucas Calhoun, photo courtesy of Nashville Repertory Theatre
John Proctor is the Villain is interesting in that it accepts the conclusion of The Crucible: that suppressed malevolence and envy can find outlet through hysterical witchhunts (literal or metaphorical), no matter the moral claims of the perpetrators. In her play Kimberly Bellflower advances another true statement: that while communities and cultures can be swept away by hysterical witchhunts, they can also hide their heads in the sand, preferrin
L to R: Advika Ravishankar, Aubrey Bagley, Norah Younger, Brityn Ramsey, photo courtesy of Nashville Repertory Theatre
The cast does a great job of embodying teenagers and educators alike: Aubrey Bagley plays Beth Powell, a bubbly character who frequently giggles, and she’s hilarious and wonderful. She made Beth into my favorite character, and I expect to see her on more Nashville stages. Lucas Calhoun plays Carter Smith, who sums up that cool teacher vibe and has great chemistry with the cast. Norah Younger as Shelby Holcomb embodies the inconsistent confidence 
The set is great, a simple classroom with two doors leading out. There are desks and chairs, beanbag chairs at the front of the stage, with the walls covered with educational posters. At the very front of the stage is a small strip of gravel scattered with leaves.
